newsitem.title: USA: U.S. semiconductor group concerned over Japan data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. semiconductor group concerned over Japan data.

text.p: The trade group for the U.S. semiconductor industry said Friday that Japan's market share data for first half of 1996 demonstrate the need for continued cooperation on trade accords.

Although foreign market share had reached an all-time high since records have been kept of 29.6 percent during the fourth quarter of 1995, the Japanese government's revised data for the first 1996 quarter show the foreign share of Japan's market actually fell by 2.7 percentage points to 26.9 percent.
This is a significant revision because Japan previously had reported first quarter foreign share at 30.6 percent.

Earlier this year, Japan had pointed to the strong 30.6 percent first quarter foreign share in arguing against renewing a trade agreement with the United States aimed at opening Japan's market to more foreign competition.

Furthermore, the U.S. Trade Representative's office in Washington, D.C., said earlier Friday that foreign market share in Japan's computer chip market fell further to 26.4 percent in the second quarter.
"These numbers are cause for concern," said Thomas Armstrong, president of the Semiconductor Industry Association (SIA) trade group.
"All year, we were operating under the erroneous impression that foreign market share reached a new high of 30.6 percent during the first quarter.
"Now we discover that the market share actually declined," he said. The SIA said Japan's government recently disclosed it had miscalculated market share during the first quarter.

The SIA said in a statement that when U.S. and Japanese officials began trade talks for the new semiconductor agreement, foreign share in Japan's market was "dropping precipitously," rather than growing.
Last summer, after tense negotiations between Washington and Tokyo, the two sides agreed to a modified plan that left to industry groups the task of monitoring market share data.

Armstrong said discovery of the error, which inflated foreign share by nearly four percentage points or around $1.4 billion in annualized sales, underscores the need for active cooperation by both sides in calculating the data.

"The Japanese government can best demonstrate that this was an innocent mistake by implementing facets of the new 1996 trade agreement in a cooperative and expedited manner," he said, adding it was too early to know if progress on opening Japan's chip market to foreign firms has been reversed.

The SIA said unprecedented fluctuations in the global market for dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips had contributed to the decline in foreign share, noting that since January, memory chip prices had plunged by more than 80 percent.
In the fourth quarter of 1995, DRAMs represented around 24 percent of the Japanese market, and this declined to 22 percent in the first quarter and 15 percent in the second.
U.S. companies were less affected by the sharp decline than non-U.S. companies, and U.S. share in the Japanese market actually increased in the first half, the SIA said.
